evidence: Caes. B.G. 4.23: nactus idōneam ad nāvigandum tempestātem (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Weather is its chief classical sense (Lewis & Short), fair or foul: tempestās serēna, idōnea, turbida. Alone it very often means a storm (see storm), and in early Latin and the historians also a time (eā tempestāte, “at that time”), so give it an adjective when you mean fine weather.

terms.gloss: the weather; the state of the sky
evidence: Plin. Ep. 8.17.1: immīte et turbidum caelum
terms.comment: The sky, and so the weather it brings, especially weather that lasts (see climate). serēnō caelō, “in fine weather”.

evidence: Cic. fr. ap. Non. 394.9: tempestās spurcissima (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: num istīc quoque immīte et turbidum caelum? hīc assiduae tempestātēs et crēbra dīluvia
phrases.english: is the weather wild and stormy there too? here it is one storm after another, and floods

phrases.latin: intemperiēs caelī valētūdinem temptat: aegrōtandum est
phrases.english: bad weather tries our health: we must be ill
having found weather fit for sailing
owing to changes in the weather
